etymology: Anglo-Saxon swetra, comparative of swete, sweet — of superior pleasantness to taste or spirit.
biblical_def:
More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb. How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!

Both uses of sweeter in the Psalms belong to the same subject: the judgments and words of the LORD, tasted rather than merely read. Psalm 19 sets sweeter beside desired, joining appetite to desire — the law is not a duty endured but a thing craved above the sweetest food a man of that age knew. Psalm 119 repeats the same comparison in the psalmist's own mouth, present tense, an ongoing taste rather than a memory. Scripture never asks the believer to find the word merely useful; it promises, and expects, that the word will in fact taste sweeter than honey to the man who has actually eaten it, not merely handled it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SWEET: pleasant to the taste; having the taste of sugar or honey; comparative degree, of greater sweetness.
webster_full: SWEET, a. Agreeable to the taste; producing a sensation of gratification, as sugar, honey, or fruit.
Pleasing to the mind; agreeable; delightful.
Grateful to the ear; soft and pleasant in sound.
SWEETER, a. Comparative of Sweet; more pleasant or gratifying to taste or feeling.
Figuratively applied to the word of God, as more delightful to the renewed taste than the sweetest natural food.
scriptures: More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb.
How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!
corruption_summary: A generation fed on entertainment has retrained its palate to expect sweetness from spectacle and stimulation, and finds the plain word of God bland by comparison — not because the word has changed, but because the taste has been ruined.
corruption_paragraphs: Where the psalmist's mouth had been trained by meditation to taste sweeter in the judgments of the LORD, the modern churchgoer's appetite is often trained by entertainment to expect sweeter from music, lighting, and novelty, and the plain text is quietly judged deficient against a standard Scripture never set for itself.

The remedy is not to make the word taste sweeter by decoration but to recover the appetite that already finds it so — the honeycomb was already the sweetest thing David knew, and he still reached past it for the word.
roots_summary: From mathoq (Heb.), sweet, used consistently in the Psalms of the LORD's words and judgments rather than of ordinary food.
roots_lines: Sweeter in both psalms describes the word of God, not a dessert.
Psalm 19 joins sweeter to desired above much fine gold.
Psalm 119 repeats the comparison in the present tense, an ongoing taste.
Honey and the honeycomb were the sweetest things available to that age.
Scripture expects an actual, tasted sweetness, not a merely professed one.
usage: Sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb — desire for the word set above the sweetest food known.
Sweeter than honey to my mouth — an ongoing, present taste, not a past memory.
Both verses assume the reader has actually eaten the word, not merely studied it.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon hwitra, comparative of hwit, white — of purer or lighter color, used figuratively of moral cleanness.
biblical_def:
Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.

David's whiter than snow, in the psalm of his own confessed adultery and murder, is not a request for self-improvement but for washing by another's hand — purge me, wash me, comes before whiter than snow, never after. Isaiah supplies the doctrine David's plea assumes: sins as scarlet, as crimson, made white only because the LORD himself reasons the case and pronounces the verdict. Whiter than snow is always the far side of an actual cleansing, accomplished by hyssop and blood in the type, and by the blood of Christ in the substance — never the product of a man's own effort to feel clean again.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from WHITE: being of the color of pure snow; free from spot or stain; comparative degree, of a purer or lighter shade.
webster_full: WHITE, a. Being of the color of pure snow; not dark.
Pure; clean; free from stain or blemish, in a moral sense.
Applied to the mind or life, as denoting innocence or purity.
WHITER, a. Comparative of White; more nearly resembling pure snow; purer.
Used in Scripture chiefly of moral cleansing granted by God, not of a natural quality achieved by man.
scriptures: Psa 51:7
Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.
Isa 1:18
Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
corruption_summary: A self-help culture offers whiter as a project of personal effort — detox, discipline, self-forgiveness — attainable by the sinner's own program, quietly detaching the word from the purging and washing David could only ask for, never perform.
corruption_paragraphs: David's whiter than snow follows purge me and wash me in the same breath; the modern substitute drops the purging and keeps only the feeling of whiteness, promising renewal without blood, hyssop, or a Judge to reason the case.

Isaiah 1:18 will not permit this shortcut. Scarlet and crimson are not softened by technique; they are made white only because the LORD himself undertakes to reason and to pronounce the sinner clean — a verdict, not a mood.
roots_summary: From laban (Heb.), white, tied throughout the Old Testament to cleansing accomplished by sacrifice, never by unaided resolve.
roots_lines: Whiter than snow follows purging and washing, never precedes them.
David asks; he does not perform the cleansing himself.
Isaiah 1:18 makes the whitening a legal verdict pronounced by the LORD.
Scarlet and crimson are the worst stains Scripture names, and both are answered.
The pattern moves from hyssop and blood in the type to the blood of Christ in the substance.
usage: Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow — cleansing sought, not self-administered.
White as snow... white as wool — Isaiah's own doubling of the same promise.
Neither verse offers a technique; both offer a Person who cleanses.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon scearpra, comparative of scearp, sharp — having a keener edge or point, apt to cut or pierce.
biblical_def:
The best of them is as a brier: the most upright is sharper than a thorn hedge. For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.

Micah's sharper is an indictment: even the best and most upright of a corrupt generation cut like a thorn hedge, wounding whoever comes near. Hebrews takes the same image of piercing and turns it entirely to good — the word of God is sharper than any twoedged sword, and its cutting is not injury but diagnosis, dividing soul from spirit and laying bare the thoughts and intents of the heart. A sword this sharp cannot be handled carelessly and cannot be avoided by hiding; it is precisely designed to reach what nothing else can reach. Where Micah's sharper wounds a neighbor, Hebrews' sharper exposes a heart, and only the second kind of cutting heals what it opens.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SHARP: having a keen edge or fine point; well adapted to cut or penetrate; comparative degree.
webster_full: SHARP, a. Having a keen edge or a fine point; fitted to cut or pierce.
Acute of mind; quick to discern or distinguish.
Severe; harsh; biting, as words or reproof.
SHARPER, a. Comparative of Sharp; more keen, penetrating, or acute.
Applied to the word of God in Hebrews as surpassing any material blade in its power to pierce and discern.
scriptures: Mic 7:4
The best of them is as a brier: the most upright is sharper than a thorn hedge: the day of thy watchmen and thy visitation cometh; now shall be their perplexity.
Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
corruption_summary: A therapeutic pulpit culture has deliberately dulled the sharper edge of preaching, softening the word until it can no longer divide soul from spirit, for fear it might first divide a congregation from its comfort.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 4:12 does not describe a gentle word; it describes a blade sharper than any twoedged sword, and a ministry that files down every sharp edge for the sake of felt niceness has produced a word that can no longer discern the thoughts and intents of the heart, only affirm them.

Micah 7:4 is the warning attached to a people who preferred comfort to correction: even their best men had grown sharper toward their neighbors than toward their own sin. The remedy is not a duller word but a rightly aimed one, cutting the sinner's excuses rather than his neighbor's reputation.
roots_summary: From tomoteros (Gk.), sharper, cutting — the comparative used uniquely in Hebrews of the living word of God.
roots_lines: Sharper in Micah describes corrupted men wounding their neighbors.
Sharper in Hebrews describes the word of God diagnosing the heart.
Piercing to the dividing of soul and spirit is diagnosis, not injury.
A discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart is the sword's stated purpose.
The same comparative degree marks both the worst corruption and the best remedy.
usage: Sharper than a thorn hedge — even the best of a corrupt people, found wounding.
Sharper than any twoedged sword — the word of God's own comparative, unmatched by any blade.
A discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart — what the sharpness is actually for.

etymology: Latin purus, pure, clean, unmixed — comparative degree, of greater freedom from defilement.
biblical_def:
Her Nazarites were purer than snow, they were whiter than milk, they were more ruddy in body than rubies, their polishing was of sapphire. Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity: wherefore lookest thou upon them that deal treacherously, and holdest thy tongue when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he?

Lamentations remembers Jerusalem's Nazarites in their former glory, purer than snow, as part of a lament over what Jerusalem's sin has since destroyed — the comparison measures a fall, not a present state. Habakkuk's purer belongs to God alone: eyes purer than to behold evil, so pure that they cannot look on iniquity at all, which is exactly why the prophet's complaint follows immediately — how can such eyes seem to tolerate the wicked devouring the righteous? Purer, applied to man, describes something lost; applied to God, it describes an attribute so absolute that it becomes the standard by which the prophet dares to question providence itself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from PURE: free from mixture; clean; not defiled or polluted; morally clean; free from guilt; comparative degree.
webster_full: PURE, a. Free from mixture; unmixed with any other substance.
Clean; not defiled or polluted.
Free from guilt or moral defilement; holy; morally clean.
PURER, a. Comparative of Pure; more free from defilement, mixture, or guilt.
Applied in Scripture supremely to the eyes of God, whose purity cannot so much as behold evil.
scriptures: Lam 4:7
Her Nazarites were purer than snow, they were whiter than milk, they were more ruddy in body than rubies, their polishing was of sapphire:
Hab 1:13

Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity: wherefore lookest thou upon them that deal treacherously, and holdest thy tongue when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he?
corruption_summary: Moral relativism has made purer a matter of taste rather than fact, so that a generation raised to say nothing is purer than anything else struggles even to parse Habakkuk's flat claim that God himself is purer than evil can bear to be seen by.
corruption_paragraphs: Habakkuk's purer eyes than to behold evil is not a preference but a description of God's nature, and the prophet's whole complaint depends on it being objectively, unarguably true. A culture uncomfortable with any purer risks losing the very ground Habakkuk stands on to question the LORD in the first place.

Lamentations 4:7 shows the other side: purer was once a real, remembered condition, and its loss was real grief, not a lifestyle choice. Both texts assume that purer names an actual difference in kind, not merely in preference.
roots_summary: From tahor (Heb.), pure or clean, and tahor eynayim, pure of eyes, the phrase Habakkuk applies to God alone.
roots_lines: Purer in Lamentations describes a former glory now lost to sin's judgment.
Purer in Habakkuk describes God's own eyes, absolutely.
Cannot look on iniquity is the strongest claim of purity Scripture makes.
Habakkuk's complaint depends entirely on this purity being real, not relative.
Neither verse treats purer as a matter of taste or degree of comfort.
usage: Purer than snow — a glory once possessed, now grieved as lost.
Purer eyes than to behold evil — the ground of Habakkuk's whole complaint to God.
Cannot look on iniquity — purity so complete it becomes an inability, not merely a preference.

pos: n. (a trumpet; the sound of a trumpet, especially at the resurrection)
etymology: Old French trompe, a trumpet — a wind instrument used for signal, alarm, or proclamation.
biblical_def:
In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first.

Trump in Scripture names one event only: the last trump, sounded at the return of Christ, at which the dead in Christ are raised incorruptible and the living are changed in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye. Paul in 1 Corinthians and again in 1 Thessalonians ties the same word to the same instant — no other trump shares the name in the New Testament's vocabulary of the end. The word carries the certainty of a signal that cannot be missed or mistaken for anything less: when the trump of God sounds, no explanation will be needed, and no one will ask what it means.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from TRUMPET: a wind instrument of martial and public use, sounded for signal, alarm, or solemn proclamation.
webster_full: TRUMP, n. A trumpet; a wind instrument of music, chiefly used in war and public proclamations.
The sound of a trumpet.
In Scripture, the last trump, or trump of God, denotes the signal of the resurrection and the Lord's return.
TRUMPET, v.t. To proclaim by sound of trumpet; to publish or noise abroad.
Figuratively, any loud or decisive summons that cannot be mistaken or ignored.
scriptures: In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.
For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first:
corruption_summary: The culture has emptied trump of its one biblical meaning, keeping only the sense of a winning card or a proper name, so that a word once reserved for the resurrection now signals nothing more than victory in a game.
corruption_paragraphs: A trump card wins a hand; the trump of God raises the dead. The distance between the two uses is the whole distance between a parlor game and the last day, and it is worth naming plainly that Scripture's trump belongs entirely to the second.

1 Thessalonians 4:16 will not be trivialized by the word's other uses: the shout, the archangel's voice, and the trump of God together describe an event no smaller word could carry, and no card game borrows its true weight.
roots_summary: From salpigx (Gk.), trumpet, used of the last trump in both Pauline texts describing the resurrection of the dead.
roots_lines: Trump in the New Testament names a single, unrepeatable event.
The last trump and the trump of God are the same signal, named twice.
The dead in Christ rise first at this sound, not before it.
A moment, the twinkling of an eye, marks how sudden the change will be.
No other use of trump in Scripture shares this weight.
usage: At the last trump — the single signal marking the resurrection of the dead in Christ.
The trump of God — paired with the Lord's own shout and the archangel's voice.
In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye — the speed with which the trump changes everything.

pos: n. pl. (shared human nature and feeling, common to all men)
etymology: Latin passio, a suffering or being acted upon — the capacity common to all men to feel, suffer, and be moved.
biblical_def:
Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God. Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain: and it rained not on the earth by the space of three years and six months.

Both uses of passions in the Authorized Version make the identical argument: a man remarkable for power or holiness is still a man, subject to the same passions as everyone else. Paul and Barnabas refuse Lystra's worship on exactly this ground — men of like passions with you, not gods come down. James makes Elijah's astonishing prayer credible on the same ground: subject to like passions as we are, and therefore not a different order of being whose example cannot be imitated. Passions here is the leveler, not the excuse — it removes the distance that would let a reader admire Elijah from a safe distance instead of praying as he prayed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from PASSION: any effect produced in a body or mind by an external agent; feeling, emotion, or suffering common to human nature.
webster_full: PASSION, n. In a general sense, any effect caused in a body by the action of another body.
In man, an effect of any external cause on the mind; feeling, emotion, or suffering.
The state of being affected by anything, especially the mind by external things.
PASSIONS, n. pl. The natural feelings and affections common to all men, without distinction of rank or office.
Applied in Scripture to establish that even a prophet or apostle shares the ordinary nature of every man.
scriptures: And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein:
Jas 5:17
Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain: and it rained not on the earth by the space of three years and six months.
corruption_summary: Modern usage has narrowed passions to mean sinful desire or, oppositely, a sacred inner compass to be followed at all costs — "follow your passion" — a use Scripture never makes, since its passions is shared, ordinary humanity, not a private oracle of truth.
corruption_paragraphs: "Follow your passion" asks passions to function as a guide to identity and calling; James asks the reader to notice that Elijah's passions were exactly like everyone else's, and his power came not from following them but from prayer offered in spite of them.

Paul and Barnabas use the same word to refuse worship, not to claim special inspiration. A generation taught to trust its passions as revelation has inverted the one use Scripture actually makes of the word.
roots_summary: From homoiopathes (Gk.), of like feeling or nature, used by both Luke and James to place extraordinary men inside ordinary humanity.
roots_lines: Passions in both texts levels the extraordinary man to ordinary humanity.
Paul and Barnabas use it to refuse worship at Lystra.
James uses it to make Elijah's prayer imitable rather than merely admirable.
Neither text treats passions as a guide to truth or calling.
The word functions as a leveler, not an excuse or an oracle.
usage: Men of like passions with you — the ground on which Paul refuses to be worshipped.
A man subject to like passions as we are — the ground on which James makes Elijah imitable.
Neither verse asks the reader to follow passions, only to share and overcome them by prayer.

pos: n. pl. (those who do good or confer benefits; here, a title claimed by rulers)
etymology: Latin bene, well, + factor, doer — one who does well by another; a conferrer of benefits.
biblical_def:
The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and they that exercise authority upon them are called benefactors. But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve.

Christ names benefactors as a title the Gentile kings claim for themselves precisely while exercising lordship and authority over their subjects — a self-conferred honor attached to power, not necessarily to genuine benefit. He does not merely criticize the practice; he forbids it to his own disciples in the very next breath, replacing the title with its opposite posture entirely: he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger. Benefactors, in Christ's mouth, is not a compliment borrowed for the church's leaders but a warning against the pattern itself — rule dressed up as generosity, authority marketed as service, precisely the inversion the disciple is commanded not to follow.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BENEFACTOR: one who confers a benefit or benefits; one who does good to another, or who contributes to another's happiness or advantage.
webster_full: BENEFACTOR, n. One who confers a benefit or benefits.
One who does good to another, or contributes to his happiness or advantage.
A title sometimes assumed by rulers or given by flattery to those in power.
BENEFACTORS, n. pl. Those who confer benefits; in Luke's Gospel, a title claimed by Gentile kings who exercise lordship.
Christ contrasts the assumed title with the true pattern of greatness, which is service.
scriptures: And he said unto them, The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and they that exercise authority upon them are called benefactors.
But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve.
corruption_summary: Modern institutional and political life has kept exactly the pattern Christ named — power calling itself benefaction — attaching the donor's name to buildings and programs while the authority underneath goes unexamined.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ's warning was never merely about first-century kings. Any leader, ecclesiastical or civil, who exercises authority while insisting on being called a benefactor has adopted precisely the pattern the Lord forbade his own disciples to imitate.

Luke 22:26 supplies the only acceptable substitute: not a title but a posture, the greatest as the younger, the chief as the servant. A church that still hands out the title benefactors to its powerful, unexamined, has not yet heard the second verse.
roots_summary: From euergetes (Gk.), well-doer, a title actually used by Hellenistic kings, which Christ cites and then overturns.
roots_lines: Benefactors was a real royal title, cited by Christ from the surrounding culture.
The title is claimed alongside the exercise of lordship, not apart from it.
Christ forbids the pattern to his disciples in the same breath he names it.
The greatest among you, as the younger replaces the title entirely.
As he that doth serve is the only benefaction Christ authorizes his church to claim.
usage: They that exercise authority upon them are called benefactors — power naming itself generous.
But ye shall not be so — the direct prohibition attached to the title.
As he that doth serve — the substance Christ requires in place of the name.

pos: n. pl. (functions of service or office; here, varieties of ministry)
etymology: Latin administrare, to serve, manage, or minister to — the carrying out of appointed service.
biblical_def:
Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit. And there are differences of administrations, but the same Lord. And there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God which worketh all in all.

Administrations, in Paul's triad, names the middle term: gifts differ, and are traced to the same Spirit; administrations differ, and are traced to the same Lord; operations differ, and are traced to the same God. The word describes the variety of forms in which ministry is actually carried out — offices, functions, appointed services — without allowing that variety to fracture the body's unity, because every administration answers to the same Lord no matter how different one office looks from another. Paul's structure forbids two opposite errors at once: flattening every administration into sameness, and setting one administration against another as though they answered to different masters.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from ADMINISTRATION: the act of administering, dispensing, or managing; especially, the exercise of an office or function of service.
webster_full: ADMINISTRATION, n. The act of administering; management; direction.
The executive part of government; those who conduct the affairs of state.
The dispensing or execution of an office, service, or trust.
ADMINISTRATIONS, n. pl. Varieties of appointed service or office, as in the distribution of gifts in the church.
In 1 Corinthians, the differences of administrations are traced to the one Lord who appoints them all.
scriptures: Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit.
And there are differences of administrations, but the same Lord.
And there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God which worketh all in all.
corruption_summary: Modern church life tends to treat administrations as merely organizational — committees, titles, and structures — losing Paul's point that every appointed office, however small, answers directly to the Lord and not merely to a chart.
corruption_paragraphs: Where Paul's differences of administrations are traced immediately to the same Lord, modern usage often reduces administration to bureaucracy: forms, boards, and process, evaluated by efficiency rather than by whom they serve.

The corrective is Paul's own structure, repeated three times without variation: whatever the administration, however humble the office, it is the same Lord being served in it. No administration in the body is beneath this accounting.
roots_summary: From diakonia (Gk.), service or ministry, the same root behind deacon — administrations names appointed acts of service, not paperwork.
roots_lines: Administrations sits between gifts and operations in Paul's triad.
Each of the three is traced to a Person of the Godhead, not merely described.
Diversity of administration is affirmed, not treated as a problem to solve.
The same Lord is served whether the administration is prominent or hidden.
The word forbids both flattening all offices and setting them against each other.
usage: Diversities of administrations, but the same Lord — variety of office under one authority.
Paired deliberately with gifts (Spirit) and operations (God the Father) in one triad.
No administration in the church answers to a chart rather than to Christ.

pos: adv. (openly, before all; not privately or secretly)
etymology: Latin publicus, public, of the people — done openly, in view of the community, without concealment.
biblical_def:
For he mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ. And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publickly, and from house to house.

Apollos convinced the Jews publickly, in open contest over the meaning of the scriptures, and Paul's own ministry at Ephesus is summed up the same way: taught you publickly, and from house to house, a single ministry conducted in both settings without contradiction between them. Publickly rules out a faith practiced only behind closed doors, ashamed of open scrutiny; from house to house rules out a faith that is only public performance with no private substance. Paul's claim to have kept back nothing that was profitable stands on both halves together — a ministry with nothing to hide in public and nothing different in private.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from PUBLIC: pertaining to the people; open to common use or knowledge; done in open view, without privacy or concealment.
webster_full: PUBLIC, a. Pertaining to the people; open to the knowledge or use of all.
Common; general; not private or restricted.
PUBLICKLY, adv. Openly; in a manner exposed to general view or knowledge; not privately.
Applied to teaching or proclamation done before an assembly rather than in secret.
Contrasted in Scripture with what is done from house to house, the two together making a whole ministry.
scriptures: For he mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ.
And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publickly, and from house to house,
corruption_summary: The age has split what Paul held together: some privatize faith entirely, calling public proclamation intolerant, while others treat publickly as performance for an audience, with no house-to-house substance behind it.
corruption_paragraphs: "Keep your faith private" is a modern demand Paul's own ministry never honored — he convinced the Jews publickly, by the scriptures, precisely because truth claims are not private property.

The opposite corruption is just as real: a ministry that is publickly impressive but has abandoned the house to house, leaving no one taught in private who was not first performed for in public. Acts 20:20 names both halves as one obligation, not a choice.
roots_summary: No single Hebrew or Greek headword; the field is open proclamation (Gk. demosia) paired deliberately with private, personal teaching.
roots_lines: Publickly in Acts describes open, contestable proclamation of the scriptures.
Paul pairs publickly with house to house as one undivided ministry.
Kept back nothing that was profitable covers both settings equally.
Neither privatized faith nor mere public performance satisfies the pattern.
The word forbids hiding the faith and forbids reducing it to a public show.
usage: That publickly, shewing by the scriptures — open, contestable proclamation, not private assertion.
Taught you publickly, and from house to house — one ministry, two settings, no contradiction.
Kept back nothing that was profitable — the standard both settings are held to.

pos: v. (past participle of broil; cooked by direct exposure to fire)
etymology: Old French bruler, to burn — to cook meat or fish by direct exposure to flame or coals.
biblical_def:
And they gave him a piece of a broiled fish, and of an honeycomb.

Broiled fish is the single, deliberately unspectacular detail Luke records at the moment the risen Christ proves his body is not a vision. He has just shown his hands and his feet and invited them to handle him and see; and then, still met with disbelief for joy, he asks for something to eat, and they hand him ordinary broiled fish and honeycomb. No detail in the Gospels does more quiet work against every impulse to make the resurrection a merely spiritual or symbolic event. A ghost does not eat broiled fish. Luke chose the plainest possible food, prepared the plainest possible way, because the plainness itself is the argument: this is a real body, in a real room, eating a real supper.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BROIL: to cook or dress by direct exposure to fire, on a gridiron or coals, without the intervention of water.
webster_full: BROIL, v.t. To cook by direct exposure to fire, on a gridiron or coals.
To subject to great heat.
BROILED, pp. Cooked by direct exposure to fire; dressed on a gridiron.
A plain, common method of preparing fish or flesh, requiring no elaborate process.
Used in Luke's Gospel of the fish given to the risen Christ, proof of his bodily reality.
scriptures: And they gave him a piece of a broiled fish, and of an honeycomb.
corruption_summary: A gnostic instinct, ancient and still current, prefers a resurrection that is spiritual, symbolic, or merely inspirational, and finds a detail as plain as broiled fish an embarrassment to be spiritualized away rather than the deliberate proof Luke intended it to be.
corruption_paragraphs: Every age has produced a version of the same doubt the disciples first felt: surely something this important cannot really be about a body eating fish. Luke's answer is to record exactly that, without apology, because the plainness is the whole force of the proof.

A faith that quietly prefers a spiritualized resurrection to a bodily one has more in common with the disciples' initial disbelief for joy than with the apostolic testimony that followed it. Broiled fish and honeycomb are unglamorous on purpose.
roots_summary: No Hebrew or Greek headword of doctrinal weight; the significance is entirely in the plainness of the detail Luke chooses to record.
roots_lines: Broiled fish follows immediately after Christ's invitation to handle his hands and feet.
The detail answers the disciples' disbelief for joy with the plainest possible proof.
A ghost, by definition, does not eat broiled fish.
Honeycomb alongside it makes the meal ordinary, not ceremonial.
Luke's Gospel builds its resurrection case on plain, checkable details like this one.
usage: A piece of a broiled fish, and of an honeycomb — the plainest possible meal, deliberately recorded.
Given immediately after Christ's invitation to handle him and see.
The detail argues against every spiritualized reading of the resurrection body.
